title: Building Production-Ready Web3 Applications
tagline: From a working demo to a launched product: control, pipelines, user experience, monitoring and calm operations
summary: The professional layer on top of the code: full-stack architecture and environments, bounded admin powers with time-locks and multi-signature control, safe brakes, a reviewed deployment script, CI/CD pipelines, transaction state machines and honest wallet UX, health checks, alerts and error budgets, staged launches and incident response. Solidity listings were compiled with solc against OpenZeppelin 5 and JavaScript was syntax-checked. This course teaches practice; it does not make any product safe by itself.

modules.title: Full-stack Web3 architecture
modules.summary: The parts of a real Web3 product, the environments they live in and how configuration keeps them straight.
modules.outcome: You can draw the architecture of a Web3 product, choose environments for each activity and validate configuration safely.
modules.intro: A demo is a contract and a button. A product is contracts, a front end, a backend, an indexer, monitoring, environments, pipelines and people who know what to do on a bad day. This module draws the whole picture and then focuses on the first discipline: keeping environments and configuration straight.

topics.title: The parts of a real product
topics.html:
Each part and its job
PartJobTypical failure
Smart contractsHold the rules and the moneyBugs, bad parameters, key compromise
Front endLet people use the contractsWrong network, confusing messages, malicious script injection
Backend and APISearch, notifications, login, rate limitsLeaked secrets, overload
Indexer and databaseFast queries over eventsFalls behind, reorganisation errors
RPC providersAccess to the chainOutages, rate limits, wrong data
MonitoringTell people when something breaksNo alerts, too many alerts
People and processDecide, deploy and respondNo runbook, one person knows everything

The contracts are usually the smallest part by size but the largest by risk: they are public, hold value and are hard to change. Everything else exists to make them usable and to notice when something is wrong. A common mistake is to spend all the time on the contract and none on the parts users actually touch.

Check what you just learned

1. Which part holds the rules and the money?
  • The front end
  • The monitoring
  • The smart contracts (correct)
  • The RPC provider

On-chain code is the final judge.

Check what you just learned

1. Monitoring exists to:
  • Write contracts
  • Hold funds
  • Sign transactions
  • Tell people when something is wrong (correct)

Detection comes before response.
keyPoints: A product is contracts plus front end, backend, indexer, providers, monitoring and people.
Contracts are small but carry the most risk.

topics.title: Environments
topics.html:
The environments a professional team uses
EnvironmentPurposeReal money?
Local chainFast development and automated testsNo
Public test networkRehearsal and user testing with the real toolsNo
Local fork of the main networkTesting against real deployed contracts and real stateNo
Main networkProductionYes

Rules for environments

  1. Every environment has its own addresses, keys and configuration.
  2. Never reuse a test key on the main network.
  3. Rehearse every deployment and upgrade on a test network first.
  4. Keep the exact same scripts and code paths across environments, changing only configuration.
  5. Make the current environment obvious in the interface for developers, for example a coloured banner on test builds.

Common mistakes

  • Sending a test transaction to the main network because the wallet was on the wrong network.
  • Deploying from a laptop with a key that also holds personal funds.
  • Different code paths for test and production, so the test proves nothing.

Check what you just learned

1. Why use identical scripts across environments?
  • A rehearsal only proves something if it runs the same steps as production (correct)
  • It is shorter
  • Providers demand it
  • It saves gas

Rehearse the real thing.

Check what you just learned

1. A fork is useful for testing against:
  • Nothing
  • Real deployed contracts and state (correct)
  • Only wallets
  • Only CSS

Realistic dependencies.
keyPoints: Use local, test network, fork and main network for different jobs.
Same scripts everywhere; only configuration changes.

topics.title: Configuration that fails loudly
topics.html:
What the code protects against
CheckMistake prevented
Required variablesStarting with a missing RPC URL or address
Known environment namesA typo selecting no environment
Address format checkDeploying a malformed address into configuration
ALLOW_MAINNET guardAccidentally running a test build against the main network
assertChainBeing connected to the wrong network
Object.freezeCode changing configuration at run time

Check what you just learned

1. Why check the connected chain id at start-up?
  • To save gas
  • Wallets require it
  • Configuration might name one network while the provider points to another (correct)
  • It makes the app faster

Trust but verify.

Tip

A configuration error caught at start-up costs a minute. The same error discovered after a transaction costs real money.

Check what you just learned

1. A guard like ALLOW_MAINNET prevents:
  • Slow blocks
  • High fees
  • Reorgs
  • Accidental mainnet use (correct)

A deliberate step is required.

Key terms: flip and sort

Environment
A separate place where the product runs
Testnet
A public network without real value
Fork
A local copy of a real network
Configuration
Settings that differ between environments
Indexer
A service that organises events for queries
RPC provider
A service giving access to chain data
keyPoints: Validate configuration at start-up and refuse to run if it is wrong.
Check the real chain id against the expected one.

modules.title: Contracts in production
modules.summary: Bounded parameters, time-locks, multi-signature control, brakes that do not trap users, and a careful deployment script.
modules.outcome: You can design bounded admin powers, put a time-lock in front of them, add safe brakes and deploy and verify with a script.
modules.intro: Production contracts need more than correct logic. They need to answer: who can change what, how quickly, with what limits, and how do users find out. This module builds a configuration contract, a time-lock, a braked vault and the deployment script that ties them together.

topics.title: Bounded admin powers
topics.html:
What the contract shows
FeatureReason
MAX_FEE_BPS constantA ceiling the owner cannot exceed, so users know the worst case
Events for every changeMonitoring and users can see changes
Custom errorsCheap and clear failures
Zero-address checksA mistake cannot send fees to nobody
Owner set at constructionOwnership starts in the right place, not with the deployer

The most important idea is the ceiling. Instead of asking users to trust that an owner will not set the fee to 100%, the code makes it impossible. Power that is limited by code needs much less trust than power that is only limited by promises.

Check what you just learned

1. What does a constant ceiling on fees provide?
  • A worst case users can rely on, enforced by code (correct)
  • Lower gas
  • Faster blocks
  • Privacy

Limits beat promises.

Check what you just learned

1. Events on parameter changes help:
  • Hiding changes
  • Monitoring and transparency (correct)
  • Saving gas
  • Minting

Everyone can see.
keyPoints: Limit admin powers in code, not just in promises.
Emit events for every change.

topics.title: Time-locks and multi-signature control
topics.html:
What each layer adds
LayerAdds
Multi-signature walletNo single person can act alone
Time-lockA public waiting period so users can exit or object
Bounded parametersA limit on what even an approved change can do
Events and monitoringEveryone can see what happened
Watch out

A time-lock is only meaningful if the owner of the sensitive contract is the time-lock. If the deployer remains the owner, the delay protects nobody.

Check what you just learned

1. Why must the time-lock own the configuration contract?
  • It costs less
  • It is required by the compiler
  • Otherwise the owner can bypass the delay (correct)
  • It speeds up changes

The delay must apply to every change.

Check what you just learned

1. A queued change in a time-lock is:
  • Impossible
  • Secret
  • Instant
  • Visible before it takes effect (correct)

That is its point.
keyPoints: A time-lock gives users notice; a multi-signature wallet spreads control.
The time-lock must be the real owner.

topics.title: Brakes, limits and the deployment script
topics.html:
Brakes and why they are designed this way
BrakeDesign choice
Guardian can pauseA fast, narrow power: stop deposits when something looks wrong
Only the admin unpausesRestarting needs the slower, stronger authority
Withdrawals stay open when pausedA pause must never trap users' money
Daily withdrawal limitCaps the loss from any bug or exploit in a day
Reentrancy guardSecond layer on the function that sends ETH

What the deployment script does well

  • Fails if required configuration is missing.
  • Uses a short delay on test networks and a long one on the main network.
  • Gives ownership to the time-lock in the constructor, not later.
  • Verifies source code on the explorer.
  • Writes the addresses to a file that is committed and reviewed.

Check what you just learned

1. Why should a pause not block withdrawals?
  • A safety feature must not become a way to trap users' funds (correct)
  • It saves gas
  • Withdrawals are free
  • It is a compiler rule

Do no extra harm.

Check what you just learned

1. A daily withdrawal limit reduces:
  • Gas costs
  • The loss from a bug in one day (correct)
  • Block times
  • Fees

Damage control.

Key terms: flip and sort

Time-lock
A mandatory delay before a change takes effect
Multi-signature wallet
A wallet needing several approvals
Guardian
A role that can pause but not move funds
Ceiling
A hard limit enforced in code
Verification
Publishing source that matches deployed code
Deployment script
Code that performs a deployment repeatably
keyPoints: Narrow, fast brakes plus slow, strong control; withdrawals stay open.
Deploy by a reviewed script that sets ownership correctly and verifies source.

modules.title: CI/CD and testing
modules.summary: Automated checks on every change, test-network deployment by pipeline, and why mainnet stays in human hands.
modules.outcome: You can design a pipeline, say what runs automatically and what needs people, and score launch readiness.
modules.intro: A team that tests by hand ships by luck. Continuous integration runs the same checks on every change, continuous delivery makes test-network releases boring, and a few steps are deliberately left to humans. This module designs that pipeline.

topics.title: A pipeline you can read
topics.html:
What each step catches
StepCatches
Compile with warnings visibleSyntax and many careless mistakes
Contract testsLogic errors
Coverage reportCode never exercised
Static analysisKnown bad patterns
Front end type check and testsBreakage in the part users touch
Dependency auditKnown vulnerable packages
Test-network deploymentDeployment script errors, in a harmless place

Check what you just learned

1. Why deploy to a test network from the pipeline?
  • It is required
  • It earns money
  • It tests the deployment script itself, repeatedly and safely (correct)
  • It is faster than local

Boring releases are safe releases.

Check what you just learned

1. A pipeline helps most by:
  • Adding gas
  • Replacing people
  • Deleting tests
  • Running the same checks every time (correct)

Consistency.
keyPoints: Run compile, tests, coverage, analysis and audits on every change.
Automate test-network deployment.

topics.title: What stays with humans
topics.html:
Automate or not?
ActionAutomate?Why
Tests, analysis, buildsYesCheap, repeatable and safe
Test-network deploymentYesNo real value at stake
Choosing the mainnet date and parametersNoA decision with consequences
Mainnet deployment signingNoA hardware wallet in human hands
Accepting audit findingsNoSomeone must own the risk
Emergency pauseA person or trusted guardianFast but accountable

Pipelines hold secrets, and secrets leak: through logs, forked pull requests, compromised actions or stolen tokens. Never give a pipeline a key that controls real value. If a pipeline can do it with a stored key, so can anyone who compromises the pipeline.

Pipeline hygiene

  1. Pin versions of actions and dependencies.
  2. Restrict which branches can deploy.
  3. Use protected environments for test-network secrets.
  4. Never print secrets in logs.
  5. Review changes to the pipeline like code.

Check what you just learned

1. Why not sign mainnet deployments from the pipeline?
  • A compromised pipeline would be a compromised key that controls real value (correct)
  • It is slow
  • Wallets forbid it
  • Pipelines cannot sign

Keep dangerous powers away from stored secrets.

Check what you just learned

1. Mainnet deployment should be signed by:
  • A pipeline secret
  • A person with a hardware wallet (correct)
  • A random bot
  • The browser

Human control.
keyPoints: Automate checks and test-network releases; keep mainnet decisions and signing human.
Never store a key that controls real value in a pipeline.

topics.title: A test strategy and readiness score
topics.html:
The test strategy
LayerTestsRun when
ContractsUnit, fuzz and invariant tests, gas snapshotsEvery change
IntegrationSeveral contracts together, including fork testsEvery change or nightly
Front endComponent tests and type checksEvery change
End to endA real user path on a local chain or test networkBefore release
OperationsRehearsal of deployment, upgrade and incident responseBefore launch and each quarter

Readiness score

Move the sliders to mark how well each area is covered (0 to 100). The score weights the areas by importance. A teaching model.

Adjust Audit and review, Tests and coverage, Monitoring, Runbooks and rehearsal and see Weighted readiness (%) change.

Check what you just learned

1. Why rehearse the incident response?
  • It is fun
  • It lowers fees
  • A plan that has never been tried usually fails when needed (correct)
  • It is legally required

Practice reveals gaps.

Watch out

A high readiness score is not a guarantee. It is a structured way to see what is missing.

Check what you just learned

1. An end-to-end test checks:
  • Names
  • One function
  • Gas
  • A real user path (correct)

From click to result.

Key terms: flip and sort

CI
Continuous integration: automatic checks on every change
CD
Continuous delivery: automatic release to safe environments
Coverage
How much code the tests run
Static analysis
Automated scanning for bug patterns
Protected environment
A place where secrets are restricted
Rehearsal
Practice of a real procedure
keyPoints: Test at every layer and rehearse operations.
Use a score to expose gaps, not to claim safety.

modules.title: Wallet UX and the front end
modules.summary: Transactions as state machines, honest messages, network handling and accessibility.
modules.outcome: You can model a transaction as states, write friendly error messages and design a front end that tells the truth.
modules.intro: Most users blame the app, not the blockchain, when something goes wrong. A front end that shows the truth calmly keeps their trust. This module models transactions as clear states and writes the messages around them.

topics.title: A transaction is a story with states
topics.html:
Why states beat spinners
A single spinnerExplicit states
The user does not know whether to waitThe user sees exactly what is happening
Failure shows a vague errorEach failure has a specific, helpful message
The app may claim success too earlySuccess is shown only when the required confirmations exist
Hard to testEach state is easy to test

Check what you just learned

1. Why show 'Confirmed' only after enough confirmations?
  • A recent block can still be replaced, so earlier success could be false (correct)
  • Because it looks nicer
  • Wallets require it
  • To waste time

Do not promise what is not final.

Check what you just learned

1. A rejection in the wallet should be shown as:
  • A scary error
  • A calm, non-error message (correct)
  • A success
  • Nothing

It was the user's choice.
keyPoints: Model a transaction as states with specific messages.
Show success only when it is final enough.

topics.title: Messages, fees and network handling
topics.html:
Good and poor messages
SituationPoorGood
Not enough for the feeError: INSUFFICIENT_FUNDSYour wallet does not have enough currency to pay the network fee. Add a little and try again.
User cancelledTransaction failedYou cancelled the request. Nothing was sent or spent.
Wrong networkUnsupported chainPlease switch to the right network. [Switch button]
Contract refusalexecution revertedThe contract did not accept this action: the amount is above your limit.

Handling fees and networks

  • Estimate and show the expected fee before asking for confirmation.
  • Explain that the fee goes to the network, not to you.
  • Detect the wrong network and offer a switch button.
  • Handle accounts changing while the page is open.
  • Show the transaction link so users can verify independently.
  • Never auto-approve unlimited token allowances.

Fee preview

Change gas and price to preview the fee a user will see. Teaching figures.

Adjust Gas expected, Gas price (gwei), ETH price (rupees) and see Expected fee (rupees) change.

Check what you just learned

1. Why show the expected fee before the wallet prompt?
  • It is required by law
  • It lowers the fee
  • Users should not be surprised by the cost (correct)
  • It is quicker

Predictability builds trust.

Check what you just learned

1. Unlimited token approvals should be:
  • Automatic
  • Always requested
  • Hidden
  • Avoided by default (correct)

Limit exposure.
keyPoints: Replace error codes with calm, specific, actionable messages.
Preview fees and handle network and account changes.

topics.title: Trust, safety and accessibility
topics.html:
Front-end safety
RiskDefence
Fake copy of your sitePublish the official address; use consistent domains; warn users
Malicious script injected via a dependencyPin and audit dependencies; use a strict content security policy; avoid loading unknown scripts
Phishing prompts impersonating your appTeach users to read wallet prompts; never ask for recovery phrases
Unsafe links in user contentSanitise and validate everything shown
Showing data from untrusted sources as if it were verifiedLabel what is verified on-chain and what is not

Accessibility and clarity

  • Use plain language and avoid jargon, or explain it.
  • Keep text readable and colours distinguishable.
  • Make every control usable with a keyboard.
  • Do not rely on colour alone to show status.
  • Support slow connections and failed requests gracefully.
  • Provide help in the languages your users speak.

Check what you just learned

1. Why label what is verified on-chain?
  • Users can tell facts from claims (correct)
  • It is decorative
  • It saves gas
  • It speeds up loading

Honesty about what is known.

Check what you just learned

1. A content security policy helps:
  • Lower fees
  • Limit which scripts can run (correct)
  • Speed up blocks
  • Hide data

Stops injected scripts.

Key terms: flip and sort

State machine
A model with defined states and transitions
Wallet prompt
The approval window shown by the wallet
Content security policy
Browser rules limiting scripts
Allowance
Permission for a contract to move tokens
Phishing
Tricking users into harmful actions
Accessibility
Usability for everyone
keyPoints: Defend the front end like any web application and label what is verified.
Plain language and accessibility are part of safety.

modules.title: Indexing, monitoring and scaling
modules.summary: Health checks, alert triage, error budgets and scaling reads without breaking provider limits.
modules.outcome: You can write a health check, triage alerts sensibly and plan capacity for growth.
modules.intro: Things will break. What separates professionals is how soon they know and how calmly they respond. This module covers the signals worth watching, how to avoid alert fatigue and how to scale the read side of an application.

topics.title: Health checks that match what users feel
topics.html:
What the monitor watches
SignalWhy it matters
Age of the latest blockA stalled chain or provider means stale data and stuck transactions
Indexer lag in blocksUsers see old balances and missing items
Alert severity: page or ticketNot everything deserves a 3 a.m. call

Good monitoring starts from what users feel: pages that are stale, transactions that never confirm, balances that look wrong. Technical signals such as CPU matter too, but a green dashboard that hides a broken user journey is worse than none.

Check what you just learned

1. Why alert on indexer lag in blocks rather than only server uptime?
  • Uptime is useless
  • Blocks are free
  • A running indexer that is far behind still serves stale data (correct)
  • Lag is invisible

Measure what users experience.

Check what you just learned

1. A stale indexer means users see:
  • Faster pages
  • New data
  • No page
  • Old data (correct)

Lag has user impact.
keyPoints: Monitor block age and indexer lag, not just whether processes are running.
Classify alerts by severity.

topics.title: Alerts, error budgets and incidents
topics.html:
Alert design
LevelMeaningExample
PageA human must act nowUnexpected large withdrawal; indexer far behind; contract paused
TicketFix in working hoursSlow lag trend; disk filling; dependency update
Log onlyRecord, no actionSingle retry succeeded

An error budget turns an availability promise into numbers. If you promise 99.5% over a month, you may be down about 216 minutes in a 30-day month. When the budget is nearly used up, slow down risky releases and fix reliability; when plenty remains, you can move faster.

Downtime allowed

Change the target and incidents to see how much of the error budget is used. A teaching model.

Adjust Availability target (%), Incidents this month, Average length (minutes) and see Allowed downtime (minutes), Budget used (%) change.

Incident habits

  1. One person leads; others support.
  2. Write down what you do and when.
  3. Pause first if funds are at risk.
  4. Communicate early, honestly and regularly.
  5. Fix, then write a post-mortem without blame.
  6. Turn lessons into tests, alerts and runbook changes.

Check what you just learned

1. What does an exhausted error budget suggest?
  • Slow down risky changes and fix reliability (correct)
  • Release faster
  • Ignore alerts
  • Raise prices

Reliability first.

Check what you just learned

1. A post-mortem should be:
  • Secret
  • Blameless and shared (correct)
  • Skipped
  • Personal

Learn openly.
keyPoints: Page only for what needs a human now.
Use error budgets to balance speed and reliability.

topics.title: Scaling reads and controlling cost
topics.html:
Scaling the read side
TechniqueBenefitCare needed
Cache values that change slowlyFewer requests, faster pagesKnow how stale is acceptable
Serve reads from your own database fed by the indexerFast, searchable, no per-request chain costKeep the indexer correct and monitored
Share one backend reader instead of each browser pollingStays inside provider limitsBackend becomes critical
Use more than one providerSurvives outagesCompare answers for important data
Paginate and limit API responsesProtects the APIClients must handle pages

Request load

Change users and polling to see requests per day if every browser polls, compared with a backend that reads each block once. A teaching model.

Adjust Active users, Polls per minute per user and see Every browser polls (requests per day), One backend reads each block (requests per day) change.

Common mistakes

  • Scaling by buying a bigger plan before fixing wasteful polling.
  • Caching data that must be fresh, such as a balance during a withdrawal.
  • Having a single provider with no fallback.

Check what you just learned

1. What is the cheapest first step to scale reads?
  • Buy more servers
  • Remove monitoring
  • Stop each browser polling and share reads through a backend or cache (correct)
  • Raise fees

Remove waste before adding capacity.

Check what you just learned

1. Caching is dangerous for:
  • Fonts
  • Static text
  • Logos
  • Data that must be fresh (correct)

Know staleness limits.

Key terms: flip and sort

Health check
A test that a system is working
Lag
How far behind a processor is
Page
To alert a person immediately
Error budget
The downtime allowed by an availability target
Post-mortem
A written review of an incident
Fallback provider
A backup service
keyPoints: Share reads, cache wisely and use more than one provider.
Remove wasteful polling before buying capacity.

Mark each page, ticket or log-only.
Write the threshold for each.

modules.title: Launch and operate
modules.summary: The launch plan, the first week, incident response, upgrades and honest communication.
modules.outcome: You can write a launch-day plan, run an incident calmly and keep operating a live product responsibly.
modules.intro: Launch is a beginning, not an end. The first days are the riskiest and the habits you establish now decide how well the product survives its first surprise. This module is about doing it calmly.

topics.title: The launch plan
topics.html:
A staged launch
StageWhat happensGate to the next stage
InternalTeam uses the main network deployment with tiny amountsNo unexpected behaviour for a day
InvitedA small group with a low capNo incidents, monitoring quiet
Public, cappedOpen to everyone with a modest capA week without issues; alerts tuned
Public, raisedCaps raised in announced stepsEach step gated on stability
Steady stateCaps set by risk appetiteQuarterly reviews continue

Cap and exposure

Change the cap and the chance of a serious undiscovered bug to see expected exposure. A teaching model with made-up figures.

Adjust Deposit cap (rupees), Chance of a serious bug (%) and see Expected exposure (rupees) change.

Launch-day essentials

  • Everyone knows their role.
  • The exact steps were rehearsed.
  • Monitoring is live before the first user.
  • The pause and the person who can use it are ready.
  • Official addresses and links are published in one place.
  • Stop conditions are agreed in advance.

Check what you just learned

1. Why raise caps in announced steps?
  • Each step limits exposure while evidence of stability accumulates (correct)
  • It looks professional
  • It is required by law
  • It saves gas

Earn trust with evidence.

Check what you just learned

1. A stage gate is:
  • A fee
  • A condition to pass before the next stage (correct)
  • A token
  • A wallet

Evidence-based progress.
keyPoints: Launch in stages with caps and gates.
Agree stop conditions before launch day.

topics.title: Incidents and communication
topics.html:
Writing to users during an incident
DoDon't
Say what happened, in plain wordsUse jargon to sound clever
Say what you do not yet knowGuess or speculate about causes
Say what users should do or not doLeave them wondering
Give the next update timeGo silent
Take responsibilityBlame others
Warn about impersonatorsAsk users for recovery phrases

Silence is read as guilt or incompetence. Short, honest updates at predictable times build more trust than perfect statements that arrive late.

Check what you just learned

1. What belongs in an early incident update?
  • A full explanation of the cause
  • Blame
  • What happened, what is known and unknown, and when the next update comes (correct)
  • A sales pitch

Honest and predictable.

Check what you just learned

1. During an incident you should never ask users for:
  • Updates
  • Patience
  • Feedback
  • Recovery phrases (correct)

Nobody legitimate needs them.
keyPoints: Contain first, then communicate honestly and regularly.
Publish a blameless post-mortem.

topics.title: Operating over time
topics.html:
Ongoing work
AreaPractice
UpgradesRehearse, review, announce and use the time-lock; never surprise users
DependenciesUpdate and audit regularly; pin versions
Keys and rolesReview who holds what; rotate after any doubt; practise recovery
MonitoringTune alerts to remove noise and add missing signals
Docs and runbooksKeep them current; new people should be able to follow them
Bounty and disclosureRespond fast and reward responsibly
CostsReview provider, hosting and gas costs monthly

A quarterly review asks

  1. What incidents and near misses did we have?
  2. Did our alerts help or distract?
  3. Who still depends on one person's knowledge?
  4. Which dependencies are out of date?
  5. Did we keep our promises to users?
  6. What will we change?
Watch out

This course teaches practice, not a guarantee. Products that hold other people's money need independent audits, legal advice and continuing care.

Check what you just learned

1. Why review near misses?
  • They reveal weaknesses before they cause harm (correct)
  • To assign blame
  • They are illegal
  • They raise costs

Cheap lessons.

Check what you just learned

1. A single person holding all knowledge is:
  • Ideal
  • A risk (correct)
  • Required
  • Irrelevant

Spread knowledge across the team.

Key terms: flip and sort

Stage gate
A condition for moving to the next stage
Deposit cap
A limit on funds the product accepts
Incident
An unplanned event harming service or safety
Contain
Limit the damage
Near miss
A problem that nearly caused harm
Rotation
Replacing keys or secrets
keyPoints: Operations is continuous: upgrades, dependencies, keys, alerts and docs.
Review incidents and near misses regularly.

capstone.intro: You have seen every layer: architecture, control, pipelines, user experience, monitoring and launch. In this final step you review a vault product the way a senior engineer or auditor would, decide whether it is ready, and say plainly what remains risky. Then take the final assessment covering the whole course.
steps: Work through the Final project: write a production readiness review lab.
Make sure every risk has an owner or an accepted decision.
Take the final assessment below.
